question: On four named binary tabular datasets (OpenML adult v2 [data_id 1590], bank-marketing [1461], electricity [151] and phoneme [1489], each capped at a stratified sample of at most 20,000 rows so that every calibration split has at least 1,000 cases), how well calibrated are the predicted probabilities of logistic regression, random forests and gradient-boosted trees with library defaults (scikit-learn 1.9.1, no tuning), and how do Platt scaling and isotonic regression fitted on a held-out calibration split change log-loss, Brier score and calibration error, with the base model held fixed?
hypotheses: H1 (replication; Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana 2005): without recalibration, random forests have higher calibration error than logistic regression, measured by expected calibration error with 15 equal-mass bins on P(y=1). Note: Fonseca and Lopes (2017) report that on Brier score, which also reflects discrimination, uncalibrated random forests often beat logistic regression; Brier is reported alongside. Decision rule per dataset (fixed now): 10 seeds; the 95% paired t(9) interval over seeds of the difference in the named metric. 'Holds' if the interval lies entirely on the predicted side; 'contradicted' if entirely on the other side; 'no difference' if it lies inside +/-1% of the reference value; otherwise 'inconclusive'. Overall: supported if it holds on at least 3 of the 4 datasets and is contradicted on none; contradicted if contradicted on at least 2; otherwise inconclusive.

H2a (contested in prior work): isotonic regression fitted on the held-out split reduces the log-loss of random forests relative to no recalibration (Brier as co-primary, reported with the same rule; ECE secondary). Decision rule per dataset (fixed now): 10 seeds; the 95% paired t(9) interval over seeds of the difference in the named metric. 'Holds' if the interval lies entirely on the predicted side; 'contradicted' if entirely on the other side; 'no difference' if it lies inside +/-1% of the reference value; otherwise 'inconclusive'. Overall: supported if it holds on at least 3 of the 4 datasets and is contradicted on none; contradicted if contradicted on at least 2; otherwise inconclusive.

H2b (an extension of Fonseca and Lopes 2017, who found isotonic helps Friedman gradient boosting on credit data): isotonic regression reduces the log-loss of scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingClassifier relative to no recalibration (Brier co-primary; ECE secondary). Decision rule per dataset (fixed now): 10 seeds; the 95% paired t(9) interval over seeds of the difference in the named metric. 'Holds' if the interval lies entirely on the predicted side; 'contradicted' if entirely on the other side; 'no difference' if it lies inside +/-1% of the reference value; otherwise 'inconclusive'. Overall: supported if it holds on at least 3 of the 4 datasets and is contradicted on none; contradicted if contradicted on at least 2; otherwise inconclusive.
Platt scaling is applied to the logit of each model's predicted probability (one input scale for all models) and reported descriptively against none and isotonic; it is not a tested hypothesis.
contribution: Seed-resolved, per-model and per-dataset evidence on four named datasets, with the base model held fixed across recalibration methods and proper scores as the primary metrics; a replication of a known calibration result (H1) and an extension of earlier evidence on isotonic recalibration for random forests and modern gradient boosting. It does not settle the disagreement among larger benchmarks.

tasks.title: Prior work on calibration of tabular classifiers and post-hoc recalibration (Platt; Zadrozny-Elkan; Niculescu-Mizil-Caruana; calibration metrics)
